questions.stem: The term 'biodiversity hotspot' was introduced in 1988 by:
questions.explanation: British ecologist Norman Myers first proposed the 'hotspot' concept in the journal Environmentalist (1988). Conservation International later formalised two criteria — (1) contain at least 1,500 species of vascular plants as endemics (>0.5% of the world's total), and (2) have lost at least 70% of its primary native vegetation. As of 2026, 36 hotspots are recognised globally.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: How many biodiversity hotspots are recognised in India as of 2026?
questions.explanation: India hosts parts of 4 global biodiversity hotspots: (1) the Himalaya, (2) Indo-Burma, (3) Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and (4) Sundaland (covering only the Nicobar group in India). Together they cover ~2% of India's area but harbour a huge share of its endemic species. The Andaman Islands are NOT formally part of Sundaland; only the Nicobars are.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Western Ghats — a UNESCO World Heritage site — is shared by how many Indian states?
questions.explanation: Western Ghats runs through 6 states along India's west coast: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu. Declared a UNESCO WHS in 2012 (39 sub-sites). It pre-dates the Himalayas geologically — 150 million years old. Hosts endemic species — Lion-tailed macaque, Malabar civet, Nilgiri tahr, purple frog. Gadgil Committee (2011) and Kasturirangan Committee (2013) proposed ecosensitive zoning.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the two criteria Conservation International uses to identify a biodiversity hotspot?

options.option_text: At least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species
At least 70% of primary native vegetation lost
Presence of at least one endemic mammal species

questions.explanation: The two-criterion test is based ONLY on vascular plant endemism + habitat loss. Mammals / birds are not required. The logic: plant diversity is the foundation of ecosystem services, and if you protect endemic-plant-rich landscapes you automatically protect most associated fauna. Many hotspots (e.g. Madagascar, New Caledonia) happen to have unique mammals, but that's a by-product, not a qualifying criterion.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot in India includes:

options.option_text: All of North-East India except Assam plains, plus parts of West Bengal

questions.explanation: Indo-Burma hotspot covers much of mainland Southeast Asia, extending into India's NE hill states (Arunachal, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura, Meghalaya), southern Assam hills and northern WB. The Assam valley floor and the Eastern Himalayan foothills are part of the separate Himalaya hotspot. Indo-Burma is famous for freshwater turtles (world's highest diversity) and primate species.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The Himalaya biodiversity hotspot is home to which iconic endangered cat found above the treeline?
questions.explanation: Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) inhabits the alpine zone (3,000-5,500 m) of the Himalayas — J&K, Ladakh, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal. Project Snow Leopard launched 2009; SECURE Himalaya is the current UNDP-supported programme. Clouded leopards live in dense lower-elevation forests; leopard cat and fishing cat prefer lowlands. Snow leopard IUCN — Vulnerable (downlisted from Endangered in 2017).
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: 'Megadiverse countries' is a separate list of nations housing the majority of Earth's species. How many countries are on this list, and is India one of them?
questions.explanation: The Megadiverse Countries list — curated by UNEP-WCMC (1998) — includes 17 countries that together harbour >70% of Earth's species. India is on it, alongside Australia, Brazil, China, Colombia, DRC, Ecuador, Indonesia, Madagascar, Malaysia, Mexico, Papua New Guinea, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, USA, Venezuela. Don't confuse this with 'biodiversity hotspots' (36 — Myers/CI concept) — the criteria are different.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The term 'biodiversity hotspot' was coined by:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: British biologist Norman Myers identified the concept of biodiversity hotspots in 1988, defining them as biogeographic regions with exceptional concentrations of endemic species facing significant habitat loss.

questions.stem: To qualify as a biodiversity hotspot, a region must have at least ___ endemic vascular plant species AND have lost at least ___ of its original habitat.
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: A hotspot must contain at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (≥ 0.5% of world's total) and must have lost at least 70% (some frameworks use 30%) of its original habitat. Current threshold: 1500 endemics + ≥70% habitat loss.

questions.stem: How many biodiversity hotspots are currently recognised globally (as of 2016 CEPF update)?
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: As of 2016, Conservation International recognises 36 biodiversity hotspots worldwide.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are biodiversity hotspots in India?
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: India hosts four biodiversity hotspots: Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma region, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands). Of the options, Western Ghats and Eastern Himalayas are the most prominent.

questions.stem: The Indo-Burma hotspot encompasses parts of which of the following countries?

options.option_text: Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, southern China, northeastern India

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Indo-Burma hotspot covers the Mekong region: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, southern China, and northeastern India (Assam, Nagaland, Manipur).

questions.stem: Which biodiversity hotspot covers parts of South Africa's unique fynbos biome?
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Cape Floristic Region (South Africa) is one of the world's six plant kingdoms and is renowned for fynbos vegetation with ~9000 plant species, ~70% endemic.

questions.stem: The Western Ghats hotspot is particularly known for its endemic:

options.option_text: Amphibians — it has one of the highest densities of endemic amphibian species globally

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Western Ghats has extraordinary amphibian endemism — over 200 species, most endemic. It also has high tree, reptile, and freshwater fish endemism.

questions.stem: Sundaland hotspot covers which island group?

options.option_text: Borneo, Sumatra, Java, and Bali (+ Nicobar Islands of India)

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: Sundaland covers the Sunda shelf islands of Southeast Asia — principally Borneo, Sumatra, Java, Bali — plus the Nicobar Islands (India). It is home to orang-utans, Sumatran tigers, and pitcher plants.

questions.stem: The primary threat to biodiversity hotspots is:

options.option_text: Habitat destruction and fragmentation due to human activities

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: Over 70% of original natural habitat in hotspots has been lost primarily due to agriculture expansion, logging, urbanisation, and infrastructure development.

questions.stem: Together, all 36 biodiversity hotspots cover approximately what percentage of Earth's land surface?

options.option_text: About 2.4% — yet hold >50% of endemic plant and vertebrate species

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: Despite covering only ~2.4% of Earth's land area, the 36 hotspots contain more than 50% of the world's plant species and 43% of vertebrate species as endemics.

questions.stem: The Cerrado hotspot is located in:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: Cerrado is the world's most biodiverse tropical savanna, located mainly in central Brazil. It is one of the 36 recognised biodiversity hotspots.

questions.stem: CEPF stands for:
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: CEPF (Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund) is a joint initiative of the World Bank, GEF, and CI that funds civil society organisations working in biodiversity hotspots.

questions.stem: The Mountains of Southwest China hotspot is the home of which critically endangered species?
questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Mountains of Southwest China (including Sichuan, Yunnan) is the primary habitat of the giant panda, the flagship species of this hotspot.

questions.stem: Endemic species are those that:

options.option_text: Occur naturally only in a specific geographic region and nowhere else

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: Endemic species are native to and restricted to a particular geographic area. Hotspots are defined by high endemism — irreplaceable species found nowhere else on Earth.

questions.stem: The Eastern Himalayas hotspot is also called:

options.option_text: Himalaya hotspot — overlapping with Indo-Burma and containing Bhutan, Nepal, northeast India, southern Tibet

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Himalaya hotspot (eastern portion) spans Nepal, Bhutan, northeast India, and southern Tibet. It is one of the four hotspots in India.

questions.stem: Madagascar is a hotspot famous for:

options.option_text: Extraordinary endemism — 90%+ of its wildlife found nowhere else

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: Madagascar evolved in isolation for ~85 million years. Over 90% of its reptiles, >80% of its plants, and all its lemur species (100+ species) are endemic.

questions.stem: The Mesoamerica hotspot covers:

options.option_text: Southern Mexico, Central America, and parts of northwestern Colombia

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: The Mesoamerica hotspot extends from southern Mexico through Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, to northwestern Colombia — including Mayan forest and Caribbean slopes.

questions.stem: The concept of biodiversity hotspots is primarily a conservation prioritisation tool because:

options.option_text: Hotspots have the most tourism revenue
Governments in hotspot regions receive aid automatically
Limited conservation funding should focus where the most irreplaceable species face the most severe threats

questions.subject: Environment
questions.explanation: With finite global conservation budgets, targeting hotspots maximises species saved per rupee/dollar — the areas where intervention prevents the most irreversible biodiversity loss.
